title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Evidence Misgrounding in Multimodal Knowledge Editing

paper.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Evidence Misgrounding in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal knowledge editing aims to update visually grounded facts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving unrelated text and visual behaviors. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding : an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence.
To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WaterBird-Edit , an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes.
Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE ( V isual I n- C ontext E diting), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence.
Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WaterBird-Edit show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. 1 1 1 Code and dataset are available in https://github.com/Wang-Z-W/VICE-main .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have become the backbone of modern vision-language understanding, encoding extensive factual knowledge about the visual world ( Li et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . When this knowledge becomes outdated or incorrect, multimodal knowledge editing ( Cheng et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) aims to update a visually grounded fact while preserving behavior on unrelated text and visual queries. Unlike text-only editing, a successful MLLM edit must apply the new fact according to the intended visual evidence rather than incidental image context. Figure 1: An example of background-induced evidence misgrounding. An edit may succeed on the original image but fail when the same bird evidence appears with a different background. Lower performance gap indicates less sensitivity to background context. However, answer-level success does not guarantee visually grounded editing. In our diagnosis, an editor can produce the corrected answer on the original edit image but become unreliable on image variants that preserve the target evidence while changing incidental context. As illustrated by the bird-habitat example in Figure 1 , an edit may succeed on the original water-bird image, yet its prediction can still vary when similar bird evidence appears with a different background. We use the term evidence misgrounding to describe this oberavble mismatch: an edit is successful at the answer level, yet its prediction remains sensitive to incidental visual context rather than being stable under changes that preserve the intended evidence. Because standard reliability, generality, and locality metrics mainly measure answer correctness, they can overestimate edit quality by overlooking context-sensitive image generalization. To study this failure in a controlled setting, we use WaterBird-Edit , a diagnostic analysis inspired by Sagawa et al. (2020) , where the edited fact is the bird’s habitat label and the background provides correlated but potentially spurious context. By decoupling bird habitat and background into four target-context groups, WaterBird-Edit tests whether an edited prediction tracks the bird evidence consistently across background changes. On this diagnosis set, we find that FT and LiveEdit ( Chen et al., 2025 ) exhibit behavior consistent with evidence misgrounding. Although these models increase the likelihood of the desired answer through parameter updates or hidden-state modulation, their predictions nevertheless remain sensitive to background changes. These findings suggest that robust MLLM editing should make the evidence used to apply an edit explicit, rather than relying solely on implicit parameter or hidden-state updates. Motivated by this principle, we propose VICE ( V isual I n- C ontext E diting), a lifelong framework that applies edits through visual in-context learning ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) while freezing the backbone. For each edit, VICE constructs evidence-summary demonstrations whose image summaries highlight task-relevant evidence and separate it from incidental context, then stores the edited fact and its demonstrations in a memory. At inference time, a query retrieves the nearest edit from memory, and a learned scope head decides whether to answer with the retrieved edit context or bypass the edit. This allows the frozen MLLM to apply edits through demonstrations designed to emphasize task-relevant evidence while preserving unrelated behavior. Our contributions are threefold. First, we study evidence misgrounding in MLLM editing through WaterBird-Edit , a controlled diagnostic setting that measures whether edited behavior remains sensitive to incidental context after controlling for the target evidence. Second, we propose VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that applies edits through visual in-context learning. Third, experiments on EVQA ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , EIC ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , VLKEB ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , and WaterBird-Edit demonstrate strong lifelong editing performance and reduced sensitivity to the controlled background shifts.

sections.heading: 2 Diagnosing Evidence Misgrounding
sections.text: We use evidence misgrounding to denote the case where an edited model yields the corrected answer on the edit image while remaining overly sensitive to incidental visual context rather than consistently following the intended visual evidence. Evidence misgrounding harms edited-model generalization, so detecting this failure can help build robust editing mechanisms. However, existing multimodal editing benchmarks make diagnosis difficult: target objects, scenes, and other visual cues are usually entangled, obscuring whether an edited answer follows the intended evidence or a correlated cue. We therefore construct a controlled diagnostic set with explicit target-context groups to test whether edited behavior follows target evidence across contexts. sections.heading: 2.1 WaterBird-Edit Diagnostic Analysis
sections.text: To make evidence misgrounding observable, we construct WaterBird-Edit , a controlled diagnostic analysis set built on CUB-200-2011 ( Wah et al., 2011 ) for lifelong editing, inspired by Sagawa et al. (2020) . We first formulate a binary VQA task: given a CUB image, a prompt such as ‘‘What type of bird is in the image? Choose from: land, water.’’ , the model predicts the species-level bird habitat label y ∈ { water , land } y\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} . Each image is also assigned a background label b ∈ { water , land } b\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} by a pretrained vision-language model. The habitat and background labels then form four target-context groups ( y , b ) ∈ { water , land } 2 (y,b)\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\}^{2} . In this setting, evidence misgrounding is diagnosed when edited predictions vary with b b even though the desired answer is determined by y y . To construct the editing samples, we first query the MLLM to be edited on the binary habitat VQA task and identify images where its habitat prediction is incorrect, resulting in 500 such images. Each retained image is then used to form an editing instance, where the target answer is set to the ground-truth habitat label to correct the model’s original prediction. The filtered editing samples remain imbalanced across the four target-context groups, thereby preserving the correlation between habitat labels and background labels that the editor may exploit during editing. For the Image-Generality evaluation, each editing sample is paired with another image of the same bird species, which we call image-rephrase sample. This paired image shares the same habitat label as the original editing image but may have a different background, allowing us to evaluate whether the edit generalizes across images of the same species. This design tests whether an editor exposed to spuriously correlated visual cues still generalizes well according to the target bird rather than the background. Details are in Appendix A . After the 500-edit sequence, we evaluate each editor on the image-rephrase samples and report: (1) I-Gen., the standard Image-Generality metric, (2) Group Image-Generality IG ​ ( g ) \text{IG}(g) , a fine-grained I-Gen. within each group g = ( y , b ) g=(y,b) , (3) Performance Gap (PG), defined as I-Gen. − min g ⁡ IG ​ ( g ) \text{I-Gen.}-\min_{g}\text{IG}(g) , and (4) sample-wise normalized probability assigned to the “water” answer among the two candidate answers (“water” and “land”): p water = exp ⁡ ( s water ) exp ⁡ ( s water ) + exp ⁡ ( s land ) , p_{\text{water}}=\frac{\exp(s_{\text{water}})}{\exp(s_{\text{water}})+\exp(s_{\text{land}})}, (1) where s water s_{\text{water}} and s land s_{\text{land}} are the model logits for the two candidate answers. A large PG indicates target-context sensitivity and functions as a worst-group robustness gap, while the distribution of p water p_{\text{water}} across groups shows how this sensitivity appears at the sample level. sections.heading: 2.2 Context Sensitivity After Editing
sections.text: We focus on two MLLM editors: FT , a direct parameter-update baseline, and LiveEdit ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , a recent lifelong MLLM editing method that modulates hidden states. The diagnostic experiments lead to the following findings. Answer-level success can hide target-context sensitivity. As shown in Table 1 , FT and LiveEdit achieve reasonable full-set I-Gen. scores of 85.2 85.2 and 83.8 83.8 , yet their worst groups are much lower, producing large PG values of 24.3 24.3 and 16.1 16.1 . This gap shows that their apparent image generalization is not robust under changes in the incidental background context. Figure 2 shows the same pattern at the probability level: for a fixed target label, changing the background substantially shifts p water p_{\text{water}} , especially for FT on water targets ( | Δ b ​ g | = 0.19 |\Delta_{bg}|=0.19 ) and LiveEdit on land targets ( | Δ b ​ g | = 0.16 |\Delta_{bg}|=0.16 ). Object-only masking provides a complementary background intervention. Object-only masking provides a complementary diagnostic by preserving the target bird region while removing the surrounding background. Table 1 shows that masking improves FT from 85.2 85.2 to 87.8 87.8 and LiveEdit from 83.8 83.8 to 92.4 92.4 , indicating that background context harms their original image-generality performance. Figure 3: Illustration of the VICE pipeline. (a) Evidence-summary demonstrations for Copy, Text-Update (T-U), Image-Update (I-U), Text-Retain (T-R), and Image-Retain (I-R), all using the same template in Equation 3 . (b) Lifelong editing, where each incoming new fact is stored together with its summary and retrieved demonstrations in Sequence Memory. (c) Inference, where a multimodal encoder retrieves the most relevant edit and routes the query augmented by the retrieved context to the MLLM when the retrieval similarity score exceeds the threshold. Together, these diagnostics show that methods based on parameter updates or hidden-state modulation can achieve strong answer-level editing performance while their edited predictions remain sensitive to background context. This observation motivates VICE , which keeps the MLLM backbone frozen and applies edits through visual in-context demonstrations that explicitly represent task-relevant evidence and incidental cues.

sections.heading: 3 Method: VICE
sections.text: Building on the above diagnosis, we propose VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that applies edits through retrieved visual demonstrations at inference time. Each edit is stored with evidence-summary demonstrations that highlight task-relevant visual cues and separate them from incidental context. Given a query, VICE retrieves the most relevant edit and uses scope-aware routing to decide whether the edit should be applied. Figure 3 illustrates the VICE pipeline.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate VICE across three multimodal knowledge editing benchmarks and two vision-language backbones, comparing against five representative editing baselines. Section 4.1 describes the experimental setup, including datasets, backbones, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details. Section 4.2 presents the main evaluation results, and Section 4.4 reports our ablation studies.

sections.heading: Datasets and Backbones.
sections.text: We evaluate on three standard multimodal knowledge editing benchmarks: EVQA ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , EIC ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , and VLKEB ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . We use two MLLMs as the backbone: LLaVA-v1.5-7B ( Liu et al., 2024 ) and MiniGPT-4-vicuna-7B ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) . Both are widely used in the multimodal knowledge editing literature and represent different architectural choices.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare VICE against five representative knowledge editing methods: FT-VL , fine-tuning the final layer of the MLLM; TP ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , appending transformer-patchers to FFNs; MEND ( Mitchell et al., 2022a ) , training a hyper-network to learn to update model parameters; SERAC ( Mitchell et al., 2022b ) , a representative memory-based method; LiveEdit ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , a recent multimodal editing baseline that modulates hidden-states with MoE modules.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Following Cheng et al. (2023) , we report five standard metrics: Reliability : whether the model produces the target answer on the edited input; Text/Image-Locality : whether unrelated text and multimodal queries remain unchanged; Text/Image-Generality : whether the edit transfers to textually rephrased and visually similar variants.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: For VICE , all MLLM backbone parameters are frozen throughout editing and inference. We use CLIP-ViT-B/32 as ϕ \phi and train only the two-layer head h ψ h_{\psi} with 256 256 -dimensional outputs. The head is trained offline for each dataset with AdamW for 80 80 epochs, batch size 32 32 , learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , temperature T = 0.07 T=0.07 , and margin m = 0.5 m=0.5 . Image summaries are generated before editing and cached. sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: As demonstrated in Table 3 , VICE achieves strong and stable performance across diverse lifelong editing setups. Its main gains appear in reliability, image-generality, and locality, which are central to visually grounded editing. For example, under 1000 1000 edits for LLaVA -v1.5, VICE improves I-Gen. over LiveEdit by 12.7 12.7 on EVQA , 3.9 3.9 on EIC , and 14.0 14.0 on VLKEB , and for MiniGPT4 , by 11.7 11.7 on EVQA and 6.9 6.9 on VLKEB . VICE is not uniformly best on text-generality, where LiveEdit remains competitive in some settings, but it maintains strong T-Gen., while giving more consistent image-side generalization and locality. More importantly, VICE remains highly stable as the number of edits increases, showing little performance degradation across both backbones and benchmarks. By contrast, the baselines reveal a clear scalability–locality trade-off. FT-VL often fits isolated edits but quickly harms locality under long sequences, while TP has limited capacity for complex multimodal knowledge. MEND and SERAC are stronger in some single-edit settings, but MEND’s accumulated updates scale poorly and SERAC’s text-based retrieval gives weak image locality. LiveEdit is the strongest recent baseline in multimodal knowledge editing, yet it still declines as edits accumulate, whereas VICE remains more stable and therefore better suited for lifelong multimodal knowledge editing. For edit, text-rephrase, and image-rephrase queries, we report similarity to the paired edit anchor; for locality, we report nearest-anchor similarity.

sections.heading: 4.3 Robustness on WaterBird-Edit
sections.text: The diagnosis in Section 2 shows that FT and LiveEdit can achieve reasonable average I-Gen. while still varying strongly across target-context groups. Applying the same analysis to VICE , Table 1 shows a different pattern: VICE reaches the highest overall I-Gen. ( 93.4 93.4 ) and the smallest PG ( 4.7 4.7 ). Its group accuracies also remain consistently high, rather than showing a sharp worst-group drop. This suggests that VICE improves not only average I-Gen., but also worst-group robustness, reducing sensitivity to background context. The observation on WaterBird-Edit consists with the main results on EVQA / EIC / VLKEB : methods with lower PG under background shifts on WaterBird-Edit generally achieve stronger I-Gen. on standard benchmarks. Object-only masking provides a complementary check. When the background is removed and the bird region is preserved, VICE remains strong ( 89.0 89.0 ) and does not show the large masking benefit observed for the baselines. This indicates that its original image-rephrase performance is less degraded by spurious context. Together, the group-level and masking results support the claim that visual in-context editing reduces evidence misgrounding on WaterBird-Edit .

sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.text: To assess the contribution of each component, we ablate the scope head, image summaries, and retrieved demonstrations on EVQA with LLaVA-v1.5. As shown in Table 4 , removing the scope head mainly reduces I-Loc., which suggests that scope routing helps prevent irrelevant edit application. Please refer to Appendix D for a detailed discussion of retrieval and routing quality. Removing image summaries lowers Rel., T-Gen., and I-Gen., showing that explicit visual evidence is important for generalizing the edit to rephrased or visually similar inputs. We also provide a discussion of the summary quality in Appendix D . The largest drop occurs when retrieved demonstrations are removed, indicating that they provide the main in-context editing signal. Overall, the ablation results align with the intended roles of the three components: retrieved demonstrations convey the edit, image summaries ground it in visual evidence, and the scope-discriminative head preserves locality. Figure 4 further supports this interpretation: the learned scope head creates a clearer margin between in-scope and out-of-scope facts, whereas raw CLIP-VL assigns some locality queries similarities close to in-scope examples, making them more likely to trigger irrelevant edits.

sections.heading: 4.5 Sensitivity to Similarity Threshold
sections.text: Figure 5: Five standard metrics under different similarity thresholds θ \theta on EVQA with LLaVA-v1.5. We evaluate the sensitivity of VICE to the similarity threshold θ \theta by sweeping θ \theta from 0.50 0.50 to 0.85 0.85 on EVQA with LLaVA-v1.5. As shown in Figure 5 , reliability and text-locality are stable across the sweep, while image-generality and image-locality show the main trade-off. A low threshold applies edits too broadly, giving high I-Gen. ( 98.4 98.4 at θ = 0.50 \theta=0.50 ) but low I-Loc. ( 75.0 75.0 ). A very high threshold is too conservative, causing I-Gen. to drop to 65.3 65.3 at θ = 0.85 \theta=0.85 . We use θ = 0.65 \theta=0.65 in the main experiments because it gives a good balance, with I-Gen. 96.9 96.9 and I-Loc. 97.2 97.2 . We also keep the same θ = 0.65 \theta=0.65 for other main experiments to avoid additional hyperparameter tuning.

sections.heading: Knowledge Editing.
sections.text: Knowledge editing aims to update specific factual associations in pretrained models while preserving their behavior on unrelated inputs. Prior work edits models by rewriting located parameters ( Dai et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022a ; Meng et al., 2022b ; Fang et al., 2025 ) , learning parameter updates ( Sinitsin et al., 2020 ; De Cao et al., 2021 ; Mitchell et al., 2022a ; Tan et al., 2024 ) , adding trainable modules ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Wang and Li, 2024 ) , or using external memory and routing ( Mitchell et al., 2022b ; Hartvigsen et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024c ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . In-context editing ( Si et al., 2022 ; Madaan et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) instead specifies new facts through demonstrations at inference time, avoiding backbone updates. To achieve lifelong editing ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) , various recent works have incorporated lifelong learning techniques ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Multimodal knowledge editing ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) extends these ideas to vision-language models. MMEdit ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) and VLKEB ( Huang et al., 2024 ) establish general evaluation protocols, while MIKE ( Li et al., 2024 ) studies fine-grained multimodal entity editing across recognition and generation tasks. MC-MKE ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) decomposes multimodal knowledge into visual and textual components and evaluates consistency across modalities. FGVEdit ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) focuses on the fine-grained editing scope of particular entities in complex images. These evaluations mainly test answer correctness, not whether the edited answer is grounded in the intended visual evidence. Our diagnostics are complementary: it keeps the desired fact fixed while systematically varying incidental background context to measure whether an answer-level successful edit remains context-sensitive. Our method VICE addresses this gap with visual in-context demonstrations and a lightweight scope router.

sections.heading: In-Context Learning.
sections.text: In-context learning ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Bu et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) enables large language models to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without parameter updates. Vision-language models can also learn from interleaved image-text demonstrations, though cross-modal interaction makes visual in-context learning more challenging ( Schwettmann et al., 2023 ) . Recent VICL work retrieves visual demonstrations and summarizes images according to task intent ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . We adapt this idea to multimodal knowledge editing: VICE uses visual demonstrations to express edited facts and a scope head to decide when they should apply.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied multimodal knowledge editing beyond answer-level success, asking whether edited predictions follow the intended visual evidence. Standard metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: a model may produce the target answer while remaining sensitive to incidental context. To make this visible, we introduced WaterBird-Edit , which separates bird-habitat facts from background cues, and VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that stores edits in sequence memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations with scope routing. Across lifelong editing benchmarks, VICE remains strong; on WaterBird-Edit , it substantially reduces sensitivity to spurious background context. These results show that explicitly exposing target visual evidence helps make multimodal edits more grounded and scalable.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: WaterBird-Edit is designed as a controlled diagnostic setting for bird-habitat editing, where target evidence and background context can be explicitly separated. This makes the evidence-misgrounding pattern measurable, while future work can extend the same diagnostic principle to broader visual facts and more open-ended scenes. VICE currently uses generated image summaries and a learned retrieval-based scope decision to expose and apply edits. These components are effective in our experiments, and further improvements in summary quality, retrieval calibration, and uncertainty handling may make the framework more reliable in ambiguous boundary cases. Finally, VICE shifts part of the editing burden from backbone updates to external memory, retrieval, and longer prompts. This trade-off preserves the frozen MLLM and supports lifelong editing, while leaving useful opportunities for memory compression, faster indexing, and more compact prompt construction.

sections.heading: Source data and labels.
sections.text: WaterBird-Edit is constructed from CUB-200-2011 , which provides fine-grained bird images with species identities. We convert the original species labels into a binary habitat label y ∈ { water , land } y\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} . We obtain the background label b ∈ { water , land } b\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} by using a pretrained vision-language model to judge whether the surrounding scene contains visible water. Specifically, we query LLaVA-v1.6-Vicuna-13B on each CUB image with a binary prompt asking whether the background contains any water body, such as a river, lake, ocean, pond, waterfall, or stream. The model is instructed to answer only “Yes” or “No”; we map “Yes” to a water background and “No” to a land background. The generated file contains one background label for each of the 11,788 11{,}788 CUB images. These background labels are used only for dataset construction and group-wise diagnostics, and are not included in the edit prompt. This gives an explicit target-context grouping ( y , b ) (y,b) , where the first component is the bird habitat label and the second component is the surrounding background. The construction is designed so that the edited answer should follow the bird identity rather than the background scene.

sections.heading: Background-labeling prompt.
sections.text: The key prompt used for assigning background labels is: Please carefully examine the background of this image and determine whether there is any water present (such as rivers, lakes, oceans, ponds, waterfalls, streams, or any other form of water). Please respond with only "Yes" or "No", without any additional explanations or descriptions. If you can see any water body in the background, answer "Yes"; if there is no water body visible in the background, answer "No".

sections.heading: Edit-image filtering.
sections.text: We start from a filtered CUB pool that contains images on which the pretrained LLaVA -v1.5-7B and MiniGPT4 -vicuna-7B fail the binary habitat classification task. This filtering produces challenging edit requests where the target answer corrects a pre-edit failure, rather than merely confirming knowledge that the model already expresses reliably.

sections.heading: Evaluation data construction.
sections.text: Each retained image is converted into a standard multimodal editing instance with one edit request, two generality probes, and two locality probes. The construction of each field is as follows. Reliability. The edit request uses the retained failure image and the source prompt What type of bird is in the image? Choose from: land, water. with the corrected habitat label as the new target answer. This field tests whether an editor can correct the pre-edit failure on the original edit input. Text-generality. Text-generality keeps the same edit image and target answer, but replaces the source prompt with a paraphrased binary habitat question. We randomly sample from the following paraphrase templates: 1. Based on its physical features, would you classify this bird as a water bird or a land bird? 2. Does this bird primarily inhabit aquatic environments or terrestrial ones? Answer with ’water’ or ’land’. 3. Identify the habitat type of this bird: water or land? 4. Is the bird shown here adapted for life in water or on land? These paraphrases ask for the same water-vs.-land habitat decision without mentioning the background label. This field tests whether the edit transfers across textual reformulations of the same visual fact. Image-generality. Image-generality keeps the source prompt and target answer, but replaces the edit image with a different image of the same bird species from the full CUB pool. Because the species is unchanged, the desired habitat answer remains unchanged. The replacement image may preserve or change the background type, which lets us test whether the edited answer follows the bird species rather than the surrounding scene. This field is the main diagnostic probe: a robust edit should follow the bird species across image changes rather than switch according to the new background. Text-locality. Following MMEdit ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , text-locality uses unrelated question-answer pairs from NQ ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) . They test whether the edit changes unrelated text-side knowledge. Image-locality. Following MMEdit ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , image-locality uses unrelated multimodal question-answer examples from OK-VQA ( Marino et al., 2019 ) . They test whether the edit changes unrelated multimodal behavior.

sections.text: The final WaterBird-Edit annotation file contains 1,136 1{,}136 edit instances over 90 90 bird species, split into 636 636 training instances and 500 500 test instances. The main diagnostic results use the 500 500 test instances as a sequential editing stream. The test edit images remain strongly target-context imbalanced, which reflects the spurious correlations present in the filtered failure pool. By contrast, the same-species image-rephrase set gives substantially broader coverage of the four target-context groups. Table 5 reports the group counts used in the test split. sections.heading: Image-summary generation prompt.
sections.text: Image summaries are generated offline and cached before editing. Following the main text, we instantiate the frozen summary model G G as a pretrained MLLM before editing; in our preprocessing script, G G is implemented with LLaVA -v1.5-7B. Given an image and its prompt, the summary generator uses the following prompt. The method section writes this compactly as G ⁡ ( i , x ) G(i,x) ; in the implementation, the {text} field is instantiated with the prompt only, without the target answer. USER: <image> Given the image and the text prompt, write a concise visual summary for knowledge editing. The summary must identify the target-related visual evidence, describe other salient objects or attributes that could act as distractors, and briefly contrast the target evidence against those distractors. Do not answer the question directly. Do not simply copy the text prompt. Return exactly three lines in the following format: Target Evidence: ... Distractors: ... Contrast: ... Text Prompt: {text} ASSISTANT: Generation is deterministic with greedy decoding and a maximum of 128 128 new tokens. The returned summary is stored together with the corresponding image path and prompt, and is reused when constructing the evidence-summary demonstrations.

sections.heading: Structured template of the augmented prompt.
sections.text: For an accepted query, the augmented prompt consists of three parts: retrieved demonstrations, the retrieved edit, and the current query. Each part follows a structured template with three fields: “Image Summary”, “New Fact”, and “Prompt”. We generate image summaries for the demonstration images and the retrieved edit image. For the current query, we instead use a generic textual placeholder that instructs the model to attend to the input real image. The complete augmented-prompt template is shown below: ... [Demonstration c i c_{i} ] Image Summary: {summary of a demonstration image} New Fact: {demonstration edit prompt} {demonstration edit target} Prompt: {demonstration query prompt} {demonstration query target/original answer} ... [Retrieved edit record] Image Summary: {summary of the retrieved edit image} New Fact: {retrieved edit prompt} {retrieved edit target} Prompt: {retrieved edit prompt} {retrieved edit target} [Current query] Image Summary: Use the given real image as the visual evidence for this query. New Fact: {retrieved edit prompt} {retrieved edit target} Prompt: {current query prompt}

sections.heading: Scope-head training data.
sections.text: The scope-discriminative head h ψ h_{\psi} is trained offline for each dataset using only the training split. For each training edit instance, we form one scope group. The reliability example is used as the anchor, and its text-rephrase and image-rephrase examples are treated as in-scope queries with the same group label. Text-locality and image-locality examples are treated as out-of-scope queries; each locality example is assigned its own unique label so it is not used as a positive example for any edit anchor.

sections.heading: Scope features and projection head.
sections.text: We encode each query ( i , x ) (i,x) with CLIP-ViT-B/32 ( openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 ). The text prompt is encoded with the CLIP text encoder. If an image is available, it is encoded with the CLIP image encoder; for text-only locality examples, we use a zero image feature. Both text and image features are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized, concatenated, and kept fixed during scope-head training. The learned head is a two-layer MLP, h ψ ​ ( ⋅ ) = Linear d → 256 ​ ( ReLU ⁡ ( Linear d → d ​ ( ⋅ ) ) ) , h_{\psi}(\cdot)=\mathrm{Linear}_{d\rightarrow 256}(\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathrm{Linear}_{d\rightarrow d}(\cdot))), (10) where d d is the concatenated CLIP feature dimension. The projected features are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized before computing retrieval similarities.

sections.heading: Optimization objective.
sections.text: Training minibatches are sampled at the edit-group level: each batch contains 32 32 edit groups by default and includes all scope examples from those groups. Within a minibatch, reliability examples provide the candidate anchors. For non-anchor in-scope examples, we use the anchor retrieval loss in Section 3 , which is a cross-entropy objective over the minibatch anchors. For locality examples, we use the margin loss in Section 3 , which penalizes cases where the maximum similarity to any minibatch anchor exceeds m m . The full objective is the same as in Section 3 : ℒ scope = ℒ ret + ℒ margin . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{scope}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{margin}}. (11) Unless otherwise specified, we use AdamW for 80 80 epochs with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , temperature T = 0.07 T=0.07 , projection dimension 256 256 , and margin m = 0.5 m=0.5 . After training, the dataset-specific head is frozen and used only for memory retrieval and threshold routing.

sections.heading: Image-summary quality.
sections.text: To assess summary quality, we audited the 500 cached summaries used by VICE for the WATERBIRD-EDIT. The audit examines format consistency and the presence of recognizable target-object and scene/context cues, as shown in Table 6 . Format consistency measures whether each summary follows the required structured format. Target matching checks for recognizable target-object cues, such as bird , beak , wing , feathers , plumage , head , tail , perched , standing and so on. Distractor matching checks for scene or context cues, such as background , water , pond , rocks , leaf , tree , branch , sky , ground , fence , surface , vegetation and so on. The results show that the summaries consistently follow the required format and usually capture both target and contextual cues. Format Consistency 500/500 = 100% Target Matching Rate 476/500 = 95.2% Distractor Matching Rate 431/500 = 86.2% Table 6: Summary quality audit.

sections.heading: Retrieval and routing quality.
sections.text: We separately evaluate the retrieval and routing stages on EVQA with LLaVA-v1.5 at θ = 0.65 \theta=0.65 . For in-scope queries (Rel., T-Gen., and I-Gen.), top-1 retrieval accuracy measures whether the intended edit is ranked first, while routing accuracy measures whether the retrieved edit is accepted. Routing errors on these queries are false rejections. For locality queries, no intended edit should be applied, so top-1 retrieval accuracy is not applicable; routing accuracy instead measures whether the query is correctly rejected, and the corresponding errors are false acceptances. As shown in Table 7 , the intended edit is retrieved for at least 97.3% of all in-scope queries, and routing accuracy remains above 96.9%. Reliability and text-locality queries are routed without errors. Image-locality queries are the most challenging, with a 5.7% false-acceptance rate, but most unrelated image queries are still correctly rejected. These results indicate that the scope head generally applies the intended edit to in-scope queries while preventing irrelevant edit application. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding : an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence. To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WaterBird-Edit , an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE ( V isual I n- C ontext E diting), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence. Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WaterBird-Edit show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. 1 1 1 Code and dataset are available in https://github.com/Wang-Z-W/VICE-main . * * footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have become the backbone of modern vision-language understanding, encoding extensive factual knowledge about the visual world ( Li et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . When this knowledge becomes outdated or incorrect, multimodal knowledge editing ( Cheng et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) aims to update a visually grounded fact while preserving behavior on unrelated text and visual queries. Unlike text-only editing, a successful MLLM edit must apply the new fact according to the intended visual evidence rather than incidental image context. Figure 1: An example of background-induced evidence misgrounding. An edit may succeed on the original image but fail when the same bird evidence appears with a different background. Lower performance gap indicates less sensitivity to background context. However, answer-level success does not guarantee visually grounded editing. In our diagnosis, an editor can produce the corrected answer on the original edit image but become unreliable on image variants that preserve the target evidence while changing incidental context. As illustrated by the bird-habitat example in Figure 1 , an edit may succeed on the original water-bird image, yet its prediction can still vary when similar bird evidence appears with a different background. We use the term evidence misgrounding to describe this oberavble mismatch: an edit is successful at the answer level, yet its prediction remains sensitive to incidental visual context rather than being stable under changes that preserve the intended evidence. Because standard reliability, generality, and locality metrics mainly measure answer correctness, they can overestimate edit quality by overlooking context-sensitive image generalization. To study this failure in a controlled setting, we use WaterBird-Edit , a diagnostic analysis inspired by Sagawa et al. (2020) , where the edited fact is the bird’s habitat label and the background provides correlated but potentially spurious context. By decoupling bird habitat and background into four target-context groups, WaterBird-Edit tests whether an edited prediction tracks the bird evidence consistently across background changes. On this diagnosis set, we find that FT and LiveEdit ( Chen et al., 2025 ) exhibit behavior consistent with evidence misgrounding. Although these models increase the likelihood of the desired answer through parameter updates or hidden-state modulation, their predictions nevertheless remain sensitive to background changes. These findings suggest that robust MLLM editing should make the evidence used to apply an edit explicit, rather than relying solely on implicit parameter or hidden-state updates. Motivated by this principle, we propose VICE ( V isual I n- C ontext E diting), a lifelong framework that applies edits through visual in-context learning ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) while freezing the backbone. For each edit, VICE constructs evidence-summary demonstrations whose image summaries highlight task-relevant evidence and separate it from incidental context, then stores the edited fact and its demonstrations in a memory. At inference time, a query retrieves the nearest edit from memory, and a learned scope head decides whether to answer with the retrieved edit context or bypass the edit. This allows the frozen MLLM to apply edits through demonstrations designed to emphasize task-relevant evidence while preserving unrelated behavior. Our contributions are threefold. First, we study evidence misgrounding in MLLM editing through WaterBird-Edit , a controlled diagnostic setting that measures whether edited behavior remains sensitive to incidental context after controlling for the target evidence. Second, we propose VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that applies edits through visual in-context learning. Third, experiments on EVQA ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , EIC ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , VLKEB ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , and WaterBird-Edit demonstrate strong lifelong editing performance and reduced sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. 2 Diagnosing Evidence Misgrounding We use evidence misgrounding to denote the case where an edited model yields the corrected answer on the edit image while remaining overly sensitive to incidental visual context rather than consistently following the intended visual evidence. Evidence misgrounding harms edited-model generalization, so detecting this failure can help build robust editing mechanisms. However, existing multimodal editing benchmarks make diagnosis difficult: target objects, scenes, and other visual cues are usually entangled, obscuring whether an edited answer follows the intended evidence or a correlated cue. We therefore construct a controlled diagnostic set with explicit target-context groups to test whether edited behavior follows target evidence across contexts. (2020) . We first formulate a binary VQA task: given a CUB image, a prompt such as ‘‘What type of bird is in the image? Choose from: land, water.’’ , the model predicts the species-level bird habitat label y ∈ { water , land } y\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} . Each image is also assigned a background label b ∈ { water , land } b\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\} by a pretrained vision-language model. The habitat and background labels then form four target-context groups ( y , b ) ∈ { water , land } 2 (y,b)\in\{\text{water},\text{land}\}^{2} . In this setting, evidence misgrounding is diagnosed when edited predictions vary with b b even though the desired answer is determined by y y . To construct the editing samples, we first query the MLLM to be edited on the binary habitat VQA task and identify images where its habitat prediction is incorrect, resulting in 500 such images. Each retained image is then used to form an editing instance, where the target answer is set to the ground-truth habitat label to correct the model’s original prediction. The filtered editing samples remain imbalanced across the four target-context groups, thereby preserving the correlation between habitat labels and background labels that the editor may exploit during editing. For the Image-Generality evaluation, each editing sample is paired with another image of the same bird species, which we call image-rephrase sample. This paired image shares the same habitat label as the original editing image but may have a different background, allowing us to evaluate whether the edit generalizes across images of the same species. This design tests whether an editor exposed to spuriously correlated visual cues still generalizes well according to the target bird rather than the background. Details are in Appendix A . The diagnostic experiments lead to the following findings. Answer-level success can hide target-context sensitivity. As shown in Table 1 , FT and LiveEdit achieve reasonable full-set I-Gen. scores of 85.2 85.2 and 83.8 83.8 , yet their worst groups are much lower, producing large PG values of 24.3 24.3 and 16.1 16.1 . This gap shows that their apparent image generalization is not robust under changes in the incidental background context. Together, these diagnostics show that methods based on parameter updates or hidden-state modulation can achieve strong answer-level editing performance while their edited predictions remain sensitive to background context. This observation motivates VICE , which keeps the MLLM backbone frozen and applies edits through visual in-context demonstrations that explicitly represent task-relevant evidence and incidental cues. 3 Method: VICE Building on the above diagnosis, we propose VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that applies edits through retrieved visual demonstrations at inference time. Each edit is stored with evidence-summary demonstrations that highlight task-relevant visual cues and separate them from incidental context. Given a query, VICE retrieves the most relevant edit and uses scope-aware routing to decide whether the edit should be applied. Knowledge editing aims to update specific factual associations in pretrained models while preserving their behavior on unrelated inputs. Prior work edits models by rewriting located parameters ( Dai et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022a ; Meng et al., 2022b ; Fang et al., 2025 ) , learning parameter updates ( Sinitsin et al., 2020 ; De Cao et al., 2021 ; Mitchell et al., 2022a ; Tan et al., 2024 ) , adding trainable modules ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Wang and Li, 2024 ) , or using external memory and routing ( Mitchell et al., 2022b ; Hartvigsen et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024c ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . In-context editing ( Si et al., 2022 ; Madaan et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) instead specifies new facts through demonstrations at inference time, avoiding backbone updates. To achieve lifelong editing ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) , various recent works have incorporated lifelong learning techniques ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Multimodal knowledge editing ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) extends these ideas to vision-language models. MMEdit ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) and VLKEB ( Huang et al., 2024 ) establish general evaluation protocols, while MIKE ( Li et al., 2024 ) studies fine-grained multimodal entity editing across recognition and generation tasks. MC-MKE ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) decomposes multimodal knowledge into visual and textual components and evaluates consistency across modalities. FGVEdit ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) focuses on the fine-grained editing scope of particular entities in complex images. These evaluations mainly test answer correctness, not whether the edited answer is grounded in the intended visual evidence. Our diagnostics are complementary: it keeps the desired fact fixed while systematically varying incidental background context to measure whether an answer-level successful edit remains context-sensitive. Our method VICE addresses this gap with visual in-context demonstrations and a lightweight scope router. In-Context Learning. In-context learning ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Bu et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) enables large language models to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without parameter updates. Vision-language models can also learn from interleaved image-text demonstrations, though cross-modal interaction makes visual in-context learning more challenging ( Schwettmann et al., 2023 ) . Recent VICL work retrieves visual demonstrations and summarizes images according to task intent ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . We adapt this idea to multimodal knowledge editing: VICE uses visual demonstrations to express edited facts and a scope head to decide when they should apply. 6 Conclusion We studied multimodal knowledge editing beyond answer-level success, asking whether edited predictions follow the intended visual evidence. Standard metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: a model may produce the target answer while remaining sensitive to incidental context. To make this visible, we introduced WaterBird-Edit , which separates bird-habitat facts from background cues, and VICE , a frozen-backbone framework that stores edits in sequence memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations with scope routing. Across lifelong editing benchmarks, VICE remains strong; on WaterBird-Edit , it substantially reduces sensitivity to spurious background context. These results show that explicitly exposing target visual evidence helps make multimodal edits more grounded and scalable. Limitations WaterBird-Edit is designed as a controlled diagnostic setting for bird-habitat editing, where target evidence and background context can be explicitly separated. This makes the evidence-misgrounding pattern measurable, while future work can extend the same diagnostic principle to broader visual facts and more open-ended scenes. VICE currently uses generated image summaries and a learned retrieval-based scope decision to expose and apply edits.
